topic.subject: social
topic.title: Electoral politics
topic.scope: why elections, constituencies, reserved constituencies, voters' list, Election Commission, campaigns, model code

nodes.name: Elections provide a mechanism for change
Reservation ensures weaker sections have a voice

misconceptions.statement: Elections are only held to choose the most popular leader.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the personality of candidates rather than the accountability mechanism.
misconceptions.fix: Elections allow voters to choose representatives who will make laws and hold the government accountable.

probe.question: Why do we have elections in a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: To see who is the most famous person in the country.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Reserved constituencies mean only people from that caste can vote there.
misconceptions.why: Confusion between the candidate's eligibility and the voter's right to vote.
misconceptions.fix: All voters in a reserved constituency vote, but only candidates from the reserved category can contest.

probe.question: Who can vote in a reserved constituency?
probe.wrong_answer: Only people belonging to the reserved caste.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The Election Commission is part of the ruling government.
misconceptions.why: Students assume all government bodies work under the Prime Minister.
misconceptions.fix: The Election Commission is an independent body that functions separately from the executive government.

probe.question: Who controls the Election Commission?
probe.wrong_answer: The Prime Minister or the ruling party.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Constituencies are drawn based on the number of houses in an area.
misconceptions.why: Students equate geographical area with population density.
misconceptions.fix: Constituencies are demarcated based on population size to ensure equal representation.

probe.question: How are constituency boundaries decided?
probe.wrong_answer: By the size of the land area.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Voting for a candidate means the voter is choosing the person who will personally rule the country.
misconceptions.why: Students merge the idea of a local representative with the head of government, so the vote seems to pick a ruler directly.
misconceptions.fix: In a Lok Sabha election voters choose their own constituency's representative (MP). The party or alliance with a majority of MPs forms the government, and the Prime Minister is chosen from among them.

probe.question: When you vote in a Lok Sabha election, whom are you directly choosing?
probe.wrong_answer: The Prime Minister of the country.

misconceptions.root_belief: Voters directly choose the head of government
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom questioning on parliamentary vs presidential systems

misconceptions.statement: A voter can freely choose a candidate only if all parties are equally strong and have equal money.
misconceptions.why: Students think choice requires equality of resources, so they doubt whether real choice exists when parties differ in strength.
misconceptions.fix: Democratic choice means voters have more than one candidate or party to pick from and can vote freely and secretly. Parties and candidates are unequal in resources, but the choice is still real. Fair, free elections aim to make it meaningful.

probe.question: Rich party A and small party B contest an election. Is the voters' choice a democratic choice?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because choice is real only when both parties have equal money and strength.

misconceptions.root_belief: Real choice needs equal resources among competitors

misconceptions.statement: Each constituency elects as many representatives as it likes, so a big constituency sends several MPs.
misconceptions.why: Students think a larger or more populous area should get more than one representative to be fairly represented.
misconceptions.fix: In Lok Sabha elections each constituency elects one representative (MP), and in Assembly elections one MLA. Total seats come from the number of constituencies, and the whole country is divided into many constituencies.

probe.question: A Lok Sabha constituency has a very large population. How many MPs does it elect?
probe.wrong_answer: Several MPs, more than one, because it is large.

misconceptions.root_belief: Bigger areas elect more representatives each

misconceptions.statement: A voter can vote in any constituency in the country in which they happen to be on polling day.
misconceptions.why: Students think voting is tied to the person rather than to the place they live and are registered in, so being anywhere is enough.
misconceptions.fix: Each area is a constituency, and a voter votes only in the constituency where they live and are listed in the voters' list. A person has one vote, cast in their own area.

probe.question: Meena lives in Jaipur but is visiting Chennai on polling day. Where can she vote in the general election?
probe.wrong_answer: In Chennai, because she is in the country and can vote anywhere.

misconceptions.root_belief: Voting is not tied to residence-based constituency

misconceptions.statement: Every citizen above 18 is automatically in the voters' list, so no one needs to register.
misconceptions.why: Students see the right to vote as automatic at 18 and overlook the need for the name to be on the list.
misconceptions.fix: The voters' list (electoral roll) is prepared before elections and people aged 18 and above must have their names on it to vote. A person whose name is missing cannot vote, so those not listed must apply to be added; the list is updated regularly.

probe.question: Ravi turned 19, but his name is not on the voters' list. Can he vote on polling day?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he is above 18 and is automatically a voter.

misconceptions.root_belief: Age eligibility alone entitles voting without registration
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT text on voters' list and Class 9 teacher observations

misconceptions.statement: The EPIC voter ID card is the only document a person needs and replaces the voters' list.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the card as the thing that grants voting and miss that the roll is the main record of who may vote.
misconceptions.fix: The Election Photo Identity Card (EPIC) is given to voters to prevent fraud and is used for identification at the booth. The name must still be on the voters' list. The card is an identity aid, not a substitute for being on the list.

probe.question: Anil has an EPIC card but his name was removed from the voters' list. Can he vote?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the card alone is enough to vote.

misconceptions.root_belief: Identity card replaces the voters' list

misconceptions.statement: Reserved constituencies are meant to give SC and ST candidates a guaranteed win in elections.
misconceptions.why: Students read reservation as a guarantee of success instead of a guarantee of candidacy, as with seat reservation in a bus.
misconceptions.fix: In reserved constituencies only SC (or ST) candidates can contest, but everyone in the area votes, and the winner is chosen by votes. Reservation ensures weaker sections get a voice and representation in the legislature, not a certain win for any one person.

probe.question: In a seat reserved for SC, five SC candidates contest. Who wins?
probe.wrong_answer: All of them or one is picked automatically without needing votes.

misconceptions.root_belief: Reservation means guaranteed victory, not guaranteed candidacy

misconceptions.statement: The Model Code of Conduct is a law passed by Parliament that sends violators straight to jail.
misconceptions.why: Students assume any binding rule enforced by the Election Commission must be a statutory law with court punishments.
misconceptions.fix: The Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines agreed to by parties and candidates, which the Election Commission enforces during elections. For example, ministers cannot announce new schemes or use government resources for campaigning. The Commission can warn, censure or stop violators during the election period.

probe.question: What is the Model Code of Conduct and who made it a law?
probe.wrong_answer: A law passed by Parliament that sends violators to jail.

misconceptions.root_belief: Every enforced election rule is a statute
